chapter_summary:
While caches and processors have become faster, main memory (DRAM) has not kept pace. Understanding DRAM technology and memory bandwidth is essential for system design.

**DRAM vs. SRAM:**
- **SRAM (Static RAM):** Uses 6 transistors per bit. Fast (1–2 ns access), low density, high power, expensive. Used for caches and register files.
- **DRAM (Dynamic RAM):** Uses 1 transistor + 1 capacitor per bit. Slower (50–100 ns access), high density, low power, cheap. Used for main memory.

DRAM is slower because it requires periodic refreshing (the capacitor leaks charge). The refresh operation consumes bandwidth and adds latency.

**DRAM organization:**

A DRAM module is organized into:
- **Ranks:** Independent sets of DRAM chips that share the data bus. A typical module has 1 or 2 ranks.
- **Banks:** Independent arrays within a chip. Each bank has its own row buffer. A typical chip has 4–16 banks.
- **Rows:** The addressable lines within a bank. A row is typically 8 KB.
- **Columns:** The addressable units within a row. A column is typically 64 bits (8 bytes).

**DRAM access procedure:**
1. **Activate (ACT):** Open a row in a bank. This copies the row into the row buffer. Takes ~15 ns.
2. **Read/Write (CAS):** Read or write a column from the row buffer. Takes ~15 ns.
3. **Precharge (PRE):** Close the row and write back any modified data. Takes ~15 ns.

If a subsequent access is to the same row (row hit), only the CAS step is needed. If it is to a different row in the same bank (row miss), the current row must be precharged and the new row activated. This takes ~45 ns.

**Memory controller:**

The memory controller manages DRAM access. It schedules requests to maximize row hits and minimize bank conflicts. Key techniques:
- **Open-page policy:** Keep rows open as long as possible to maximize row hits.
- **Close-page policy:** Precharge rows immediately after access to minimize latency for random accesses.
- **Bank interleaving:** Spread consecutive memory addresses across different banks to allow parallel access.
- **Request reordering:** Reorder memory requests to maximize row hits and minimize bank conflicts.

**Memory bandwidth:**

Memory bandwidth is the rate at which data can be transferred between memory and the processor. It is determined by:
- **Data bus width:** Typically 64 bits (8 bytes) per channel.
- **Data rate:** DDR4 runs at 3200 MT/s (million transfers per second), which is 25.6 GB/s per channel. DDR5 runs at 6400 MT/s, which is 51.2 GB/s per channel.
- **Number of channels:** Modern processors have 2–8 memory channels. A quad-channel DDR4 system provides 102.4 GB/s.

**Bandwidth vs. latency:**

Bandwidth and latency are different. Bandwidth is the total data transfer rate. Latency is the time for a single access. A system can have high bandwidth but high latency (e.g., many slow channels in parallel) or low bandwidth but low latency (e.g., one fast channel).

**Memory bandwidth as a bottleneck:**

For bandwidth-bound workloads (e.g., streaming data, graphics, AI), memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. If the processor can execute 100 GFLOPS but memory bandwidth is only 50 GB/s, and each FLOP requires 1 byte of data, the effective performance is limited to 50 GFLOPS.

**High Bandwidth Memory (HBM):**

HBM is a 3D-stacked DRAM technology that provides much higher bandwidth than traditional DDR. HBM stacks multiple DRAM dies on top of each other and connects them with through-silicon vias (TSVs). HBM2 provides 307 GB/s per stack, and HBM3 provides 819 GB/s. HBM is used in GPUs (NVIDIA A100, H100) and high-performance processors (AMD MI300).

**Trade-offs:**
- **DDR:** Lower bandwidth, higher capacity, lower cost, higher latency. Good for general-purpose systems.
- **HBM:** Higher bandwidth, lower capacity, higher cost, lower latency. Good for bandwidth-bound accelerators.
- **LPDDR:** Low-power DDR for mobile devices. Balances bandwidth and power.

screens.title: Memory Bandwidth and DRAM Technology
screens.subtitle: Why DRAM, organization, bandwidth limits, and when HBM matters

narration.text: In this lesson we will build an actionable understanding of DRAM and memory bandwidth, and why these topics matter for real systems. You will learn what makes DRAM different from the fast SRAM in caches, how banks, rows, and columns are organized, and how the memory controller schedules accesses to reduce costly row changes. We will connect those micro details to system-level limits: data bus width, transfers per second, and the number of memory channels that together define peak bandwidth. You will also see how bandwidth differs from latency, why bandwidth becomes the bottleneck for streaming and AI workloads, and when High Bandwidth Memory is the right choice. A concrete calculation will show you how to compute theoretical GB per second for real configurations, and then we compare that to the bandwidth needed by matrix multiply and a training workload. By the end you will be able to reason about trade-offs between capacity, cost, and bandwidth and to spot when the memory system, not the C P U, is the limiting factor. Think of this as learning the librarian's rules for feeding a hungry processor.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: DRAM provides dense main memory but is slower than SRAM; memory bandwidth and controller policies determine how well processors are fed and when bandwidth becomes a bottleneck.

screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how DRAM stores bits and why it is slower than SRAM, and to describe how ranks, banks, rows and columns form the addressable structure of a module. You will also be able to define memory bandwidth and calculate theoretical GB per second from bus width, transfer rate, and channel count. Finally you will analyze the common trade-offs between capacity, latency and bandwidth, and reason about when HBM or DDR is the right choice. Each objective focuses on practical reasoning: for example, explaining why a row hit is fast and why bank conflicts reduce throughput, or computing whether a given G P U with HBM stacks can feed peak compute for an AI workload. These are skills you will use when interpreting profiler output, designing experiments with stream-style benchmarks, or choosing memory for accelerators. The objectives are verified by small calculations and explanations that connect micro-level DRAM behavior to system-level performance outcomes.

screens.title: Why DRAM matters: the memory performance gap
screens.subtitle: Caches and processors have outpaced main memory

narration.text: Modern processors and their cache hierarchies have become extremely fast and can deliver millions of instructions per second, but main memory has not scaled at the same rate. This mismatch creates a memory performance gap: the C P U can often wait on DRAM to provide data. DRAM is designed for density and cost-effectiveness using one transistor and one capacitor per bit. That design gives high capacity and low cost per bit but requires periodic refresh because capacitors leak charge. Refresh cycles consume time on the memory bus and add latency, reducing effective bandwidth. The practical consequence is that system designers must think in two dimensions: how many bytes per second the system can move (bandwidth) and how long a single access takes (latency). For streaming workloads bandwidth is the limiting factor; for pointer-chasing workloads latency dominates. A common misconception is to treat high peak GB/s as a guarantee of fast small accesses. In reality, a system can have high aggregate bandwidth and still show long latencies for single requests. To reason about performance you will need both bandwidth calculations and an understanding of DRAM behavior under realistic access patterns.

keyIdea.title: Memory performance gap
keyIdea.text: Processors can be starved by slow main memory; DRAM design favors density and cost over single-access speed, creating distinct bandwidth and latency considerations.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Why DRAM matters
Definition

DRAM is main memory optimized for density using one capacitor and one transistor per bit. It trades access speed for capacity and cost.

Concrete example

A server may have hundreds of gigabytes of DRAM but each random access can take tens of nanoseconds, while an L1 cache access is on the order of 1–2 ns.

Common misconception

High peak bandwidth does not guarantee low latency for single random accesses; they are separate metrics and both matter depending on workload.

Key Takeaway

Understand whether your workload needs sustained GB/s or low single-access latency before choosing memory technology.

Illustration: library analogy
Shelf = row
Room = bank
Librarian = controller
Reading many books from the same shelf is fast (row hit). Moving to a new shelf requires closing and opening operations that add delay (row miss).

screens.title: DRAM versus SRAM
screens.subtitle: Cell structure, speed, density, power and cost

narration.text: Let's contrast DRAM and SRAM so you see the engineering trade-offs. SRAM uses six transistors per bit in a latch-like arrangement, which makes it very fast — on the order of one to two nanoseconds for access — but it consumes a lot of silicon area and power per bit. That is why caches and register files use SRAM: they need very fast access and can pay the area and cost. DRAM instead uses a single transistor and one capacitor per bit. The capacitor stores charge and represents the bit; because it leaks, DRAM rows must be periodically refreshed. Typical DRAM access times are much higher — tens of nanoseconds — but its density is far greater, making it economical for main memory. The refresh operation costs bandwidth and imposes additional latency. An important practical point is power: while a single DRAM bit is cheaper and lower static power than many SRAM cells, the need to refresh and to drive wide buses makes system power nontrivial. A common misconception is thinking DRAM is simply slower SRAM; instead, DRAM is lower-cost and higher-density with refresh-driven constraints that shape performance. Knowing these differences helps in choosing memory for caches, main memory, or accelerators.

keyIdea.title: SRAM vs DRAM
keyIdea.text: SRAM is fast and sparse; DRAM is dense and economical but slower and refresh-dependent. Use SRAM for caches, DRAM for main memory.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › DRAM vs SRAM
Comparison table
SRAM (Caches)
  • 6 transistors / bit
  • Access ~1–2 ns
  • Low latency, high power, high cost
  • Used for L1/L2 caches
DRAM (Main memory)
  • 1 transistor + 1 capacitor / bit
  • Access ~50–100 ns
  • High density, low cost, needs refresh
  • Used for system memory
Example: caches use SRAM because they must deliver single-cycle hits; DRAM is used when capacity per dollar matters even though single-access latency is higher.
Refresh and bandwidth cost

DRAM capacitors leak and require periodic refresh. Refresh cycles consume time and can block accesses, reducing effective bandwidth and increasing apparent latency. System designers must budget for refresh when estimating usable GB/s.

Common mistake

Treating DRAM as a simple slower SRAM ignores refresh and bus contention effects that reduce effective throughput.

screens.title: Ranks, banks, rows and columns
screens.subtitle: How a DRAM module is structured for parallelism

narration.text: DRAM modules are hierarchical to enable parallelism and to map addresses efficiently. At the top level, ranks are independent sets of chips that share a data bus; a module commonly has one or two ranks. Within each chip, banks are independent arrays that can be activated in parallel. Each bank contains rows and columns. A row is a long contiguous line of bits — typically on the order of several kilobytes (an example row might be around 8 KB). Columns select smaller units within the active row, typically 64 bits or 8 bytes per column access. Each bank also has a row buffer: when you activate a row, its data is copied into the bank's row buffer so subsequent reads or writes to that row are fast. The organization matters because spreading consecutive addresses across banks is a primary way to increase parallelism. Conversely, many accesses to different rows within the same bank force repeated precharge and activate sequences and reduce throughput. Thinking in terms of ranks, banks, rows and columns helps you design address interleaving and understand where contention will occur in a real memory system.

keyIdea.title: Organization matters
keyIdea.text: Ranks and banks create parallelism; rows and columns determine the granularity of activation and the role of row buffers in access speed.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › DRAM Organization
Hierarchy cards
Ranks
Independent sets of chips sharing the data bus; modules commonly have 1–2 ranks.
Banks
Independent arrays inside a chip, each with its own row buffer allowing parallel accesses across banks.
Rows & Columns
Rows are large addressable lines (e.g., ~8 KB); columns select smaller pieces (usually 64 bits) from a row buffer.
Practical implication
  • Interleaving addresses across banks lets multiple banks be active and transfer data simultaneously.
  • Many accesses to different rows in the same bank cause repeated activate and precharge steps, lowering throughput.
  • A good memory system maps hot, consecutive addresses to different banks to exploit parallelism.
Analogy: think of banks as rooms and rows as shelves inside those rooms. You can read from multiple rooms in parallel, but switching shelves in the same room is costly.

screens.title: Rows, columns and the row buffer
screens.subtitle: Why activating a row matters and what a row hit gives you

narration.text: When you access DRAM you don't directly read a single byte from a random physical capacitor. Instead, the controller issues an activate command that opens an entire row and copies it into the bank's row buffer. After activation, reads or writes to columns within that row come from the buffer and are much faster than opening a new row. The typical sequence is activate, then read or write (CAS), then precharge to close the row. Roughly speaking, each of those steps takes on the order of 15 nanoseconds, so an access that requires activate plus CAS plus precharge is noticeably slower than a row hit that only needs CAS. A row hit occurs when the next access targets data already present in the row buffer; in that case the expensive activate and precharge steps can be avoided. A common misconception is that all memory accesses are equally costly; in DRAM, locality within the same row makes many consecutive accesses much cheaper. In practice, memory controllers schedule requests to increase row hits where possible, but they must also avoid starving other requesters. Remember: the row buffer is the key to turning long DRAM arrays into fast repeated accesses for local patterns.

keyIdea.title: Row buffer benefit
keyIdea.text: Opening a row into the row buffer enables faster repeated column accesses (row hits); switching rows costs extra activate and precharge time.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Rows, columns & row buffer
Access sequence
1. Activate (ACT): open a row and copy it into the row buffer (~15 ns).
2. Read/Write (CAS): access columns from the row buffer (~15 ns for the command/latency).
3. Precharge (PRE): close the row and write back modified data (~15 ns).
If the next access targets the same row, only CAS is needed. If it targets a different row in the same bank, precharge + activate + CAS are required, adding roughly 45 ns total compared to a hit.
Concrete example

Reading four consecutive columns in a row after a single activate is much faster than performing four separate accesses that each change rows. This is why spatial locality in programs maps well to DRAM row buffers.

Pro tip

Arrange hot data so consecutive accesses fall within the same row or across different banks to exploit row hits and parallelism.

screens.title: DRAM access timing: ACT, CAS, PRE
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step costs and the impact of row misses

narration.text: Let's walk through the typical DRAM access flow and the timing impact of each step. First, the controller issues an ACTIVATE command to copy a full row into the row buffer. This operation prepares the bank for access and commonly takes on the order of 15 nanoseconds. Next, the controller issues a read or write command — often called column access or CAS — which specifies the column offset within the row and reads or writes the selected bytes; this step also costs on the order of 15 ns for the command and data transfer latency. Finally, when the bank needs to serve a different row, the controller issues PRECHARGE to close the current row and prepare the bank for the next activation; PRE typically costs another ~15 ns. If a request targets the same row already in the buffer, only CAS is needed and the effective latency is much lower. If the access targets a different row in the same bank, the sequence PRE + ACT + CAS adds up and can be roughly three times slower than a row hit. A misconception is assuming DRAM timings are constant; in reality they depend on whether a row is open and whether banks are conflicted, which makes scheduling and locality crucial for performance.

keyIdea.title: Access steps
keyIdea.text: ACT, CAS and PRE are the key timed steps in DRAM. Row hits avoid activate/precharge and thus are much faster than row misses.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › DRAM Access Timing
Step timeline
Activate (ACT)
Open row into row buffer. ~15 ns.
Read/Write (CAS)
Access column data from row buffer. ~15 ns.
Precharge (PRE)
Close row and prepare bank for next ACT. ~15 ns.
Illustrative comparison
A row hit: single CAS (~15 ns). A row miss in same bank: PRE + ACT + CAS (~45 ns). This gap explains why locality and controller scheduling have outsized effects on observed latency and throughput.
Check your understanding

If many requests hit the same row, what happens to effective latency and bandwidth? If requests frequently switch rows in one bank, what is the effect?

screens.title: Row hits, row misses and bank conflicts
screens.subtitle: How access patterns change throughput

narration.text: Row hits, row misses, and bank conflicts are the primary micro-behaviors that shape DRAM throughput. A row hit occurs when the requested address is in the bank's currently open row, allowing only a column access and thus low latency. A row miss happens when the required data is in a different row of that same bank; the current row must be precharged and the new row activated, adding roughly two extra timed steps. Bank conflicts refer to situations where multiple outstanding accesses target the same bank but different rows, forcing serialized precharge/activate cycles instead of parallel transfers. You can avoid bank conflicts by interleaving consecutive addresses across banks so different banks can service requests simultaneously. A common misconception is blaming low measured bandwidth only on bus width or transfer rate; often the true cause is poor access locality that causes excessive row misses and bank conflicts. A practical example: streaming sequential memory typically yields many row hits in the same row buffer if the row size and access stride align, producing high effective bandwidth. Random accesses that jump across rows and banks will show much lower throughput even if the peak GB/s metric is high.

keyIdea.title: Pattern matters
keyIdea.text: Access locality and bank mapping determine whether you see row hits and parallel bank transfers or costly row misses and conflicts that reduce throughput.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Row hits vs misses
Side-by-side
Row hit
Only CAS required. Low latency, high throughput for repeated accesses in a row.
Row miss
PRE + ACT + CAS required. Higher latency and lower effective throughput.
Bank conflicts serialize accesses that could otherwise proceed in parallel across banks; interleaving addresses across banks reduces these conflicts.
Example scenario

If two threads repeatedly access different rows in the same bank, they will experience many row misses and stall each other. If their data is interleaved across separate banks, both banks can serve requests in parallel and overall throughput rises.

Misconception

Higher peak bus speed does not fix bank-level serialization; scheduling and data layout are often the limiting factor.

screens.title: Memory controller strategies
screens.subtitle: Open-page, close-page, interleaving and request reordering

narration.text: The memory controller is the librarian of DRAM requests. Its job is to schedule activates, reads, writes and precharges to deliver good overall throughput while maintaining fairness for different requesters. Several simple policies are common. The open-page policy keeps a row open after access, which maximizes the chance of subsequent row hits and benefits workloads with strong spatial locality. The close-page policy precharges a row immediately after access, which helps random-access workloads because the bank is ready for an activation to a different row without delay. Bank interleaving maps consecutive addresses to different banks so that sequential accesses can proceed in parallel across banks. Request reordering rearranges queued requests to maximize row hits or to minimize bank conflicts; this improves aggregate throughput but can increase latency for some individual requests. Controllers therefore often implement quality-of-service controls to prioritize latency-sensitive C P U requests over background DMA traffic. A common misconception is that the controller always prefers maximum throughput; in practice, it balances throughput, latency, and fairness according to system goals. Memory controller strategies means controllers use open/close policies, interleaving and reordering to trade between throughput and latency; qos is used to balance fairness and priorities.. In practical terms, open-page, close-page, interleaving and request reordering. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Controller trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Controllers use open/close policies, interleaving and reordering to trade between throughput and latency; QoS is used to balance fairness and priorities.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Memory Controller
Policies
Open-page: keep row open to favor locality and increase row hits.
Close-page: precharge immediately to reduce latency for random accesses.
Bank interleaving: distribute addresses across banks to enable parallel transfers.
Request reordering: reorder to improve row hits but may delay some requests.
Practical example

If the queue contains requests to rows A, B, A in the same bank, reordering to A, A, B yields two row hits instead of two misses. But that reordering can increase latency for the B requester. Controllers therefore mix throughput optimization with QoS rules to prevent starvation.

Check your understanding

Why might a controller choose close-page for a database workload and open-page for a streaming workload?

screens.title: Memory bandwidth: what it is and how to compute it
screens.subtitle: Data bus width, transfer rate and channels determine peak GB/s

narration.text: Memory bandwidth is the maximum rate at which data can move between DRAM and the processor, usually measured in gigabytes per second. Three factors determine peak theoretical bandwidth: the data bus width (commonly 64 bits or 8 bytes per channel), the data rate in million transfers per second (MT/s), and the number of independent memory channels. Multiply bytes per transfer by transfers per second to get per-channel GB/s, then multiply by channel count for total system bandwidth. For example, DDR4-3200 is often quoted as 3200 MT/s and with an 8-byte bus that equals 25.6 GB/s per channel. A dual-channel system would double that to 51.2 GB/s. DDR5 at higher rates increases per-channel GB/s; additional channels multiply the total throughput linearly. A common misunderstanding is to treat theoretical peak as the sustained rate; real workloads may achieve less because of bank conflicts, refresh, and controller overhead. You will later apply these formulas to compute whether a system can sustain the data rate required by specific workloads like matrix multiplication or training samples per second. Memory bandwidth: what it is and how to compute it means peak gb/s = channels × bytes per transfer × transfers per second. real sustained bandwidth is often lower due to dram behavior and controller overhead.. In practical terms, data bus width, transfer rate and channels determine peak gb/s. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bandwidth formula
keyIdea.text: Peak GB/s = channels × bytes per transfer × transfers per second. Real sustained bandwidth is often lower due to DRAM behavior and controller overhead.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Memory Bandwidth
Formula
Per-channel GB/s = bytes per transfer × transfers per second. Total GB/s = per-channel GB/s × number of channels.
Example: DDR4-3200
8 bytes × 3200M = 25.6 GB/s per channel.
Dual-channel total
25.6 × 2 = 51.2 GB/s.
Real factors that reduce sustained bandwidth
  • Refresh cycles that consume bus time.
  • Row misses and bank conflicts that serialize transfers.
  • Controller overhead and request reordering effects.

narration.text: Now we perform the hands-on theoretical calculations the chapter proposes. The rule is simple: multiply bytes per transfer (8 for a 64-bit bus) by the MT/s rate to get per-channel GB per second, then multiply by number of channels. For dual-channel DDR4-3200: per-channel is 8 bytes × 3200 million = 25.6 GB/s; with two channels the system peak is 51.2 GB/s. For quad-channel DDR5-5600: per-channel is 8 bytes × 5600 million = 44.8 GB/s; with four channels the peak is 179.2 GB/s. For HBM2E with four stacks, each stack is 307 GB/s, so 4 × 307 = 1,228 GB/s. These are theoretical peaks; later we compare to workload needs. A common mistake is forgetting to convert bytes and transfers into the same units or to multiply by channel count. Use these formulas to get consistent GB/s numbers you can compare against the data movement required by your workload. Compute theoretical memory bandwidth means apply bytes × mt/s × channels to compute peak gb/s: e.g., dual ddr4-3200 = 51.2 gb/s; quad ddr5-5600 = 179.2 gb/s; 4×hbm2e = 1,228 gb/s.. In practical terms, example calculations for given systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Theoretical peaks
keyIdea.text: Apply bytes × MT/s × channels to compute peak GB/s: e.g., dual DDR4-3200 = 51.2 GB/s; quad DDR5-5600 = 179.2 GB/s; 4×HBM2E = 1,228 GB/s.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Theoretical Bandwidth
Calculations (exact)
// Dual-channel DDR4-3200
bytes_per_transfer = 8                      // 64-bit bus = 8 bytes
per_channel_rate = 3200e6                  // 3200 MT/s
per_channel_gb_s = (bytes_per_transfer * per_channel_rate) / 1e9
// per_channel_gb_s = 25.6
system_channels = 2
total_gb_s = per_channel_gb_s * system_channels
// total_gb_s = 51.2 GB/s

// Quad-channel DDR5-5600
bytes_per_transfer = 8
per_channel_rate = 5600e6
per_channel_gb_s = (bytes_per_transfer * per_channel_rate) / 1e9
// per_channel_gb_s = 44.8
system_channels = 4
total_gb_s = per_channel_gb_s * system_channels
// total_gb_s = 179.2 GB/s

// HBM2E with 4 stacks
per_stack_gb_s = 307
stacks = 4
total_gb_s = per_stack_gb_s * stacks
// total_gb_s = 1228 GB/s
Notes
  • These are theoretical peak numbers; sustained bandwidth will be lower due to refresh, conflicts, and controller overhead.
  • Keep units consistent: bytes, transfers per second, and channels.

screens.title: Workload bandwidth requirements
screens.subtitle: Matrix multiply and neural network examples

narration.text: We now compute the bandwidth that two example workloads would require and compare that to system peaks. First, a conventional dense matrix multiplication of two 4096 by 4096 matrices typically requires on the order of 2 × N^3 floating-point operations, which for N = 4096 gives about 137.4 billion FLOPs. Using the chapter's assumption that each FLOP requires 2 bytes of memory traffic, total memory traffic for one multiplication is roughly 274.9 billion bytes, or about 274.9 GB. If you wanted to complete that multiplication in one second, you would need about 274.9 GB/s of sustained memory bandwidth. Second, consider training with batch size 32 where each sample requires 602,112 bytes. At 1,000 samples per second the total memory traffic is 602,112,000 bytes per second, about 0.602 GB/s. If the measurement is per batch, multiply by batches per second accordingly. Comparing these numbers to system peaks: dual DDR4-3200 at 51.2 GB/s is insufficient to stream a 4096-matrix multiply in one second; HBM stacks can supply much higher GB/s. A common mistake is to compare total data for an operation to peak GB/s without converting to a time unit; always compute bytes per second when deciding if a system is bandwidth-limited.

keyIdea.title: Workload vs system
keyIdea.text: Matrix multiplication of 4096 matrices needs ~275 GB for one run; to do it in one second requires ~275 GB/s. Small-sample training at 1,000 samples/s may require ~0.6 GB/s.

N = 4096
flops ≈ 2 * N**3                          // ≈ 137,438,953,472 FLOPs
bytes_per_flop = 2                        // assumption from chapter
total_bytes = flops * bytes_per_flop     // ≈ 274,877,906,944 bytes ≈ 274.9 GB
// If performed in 1 second: required bandwidth ≈ 274.9 GB/s
Neural network training example
bytes_per_sample = 602112
samples_per_second = 1000
total_bytes_per_second = bytes_per_sample * samples_per_second
// 602,112,000 bytes/s ≈ 0.602 GB/s

screens.title: DDR, HBM and LPDDR trade-offs
screens.subtitle: Capacity, bandwidth, cost and use cases

narration.text: Different DRAM technologies exist to meet different system needs. DDR variants (DDR4, DDR5) provide moderate to high capacity at relatively low cost. They are suitable for general-purpose systems where total memory capacity and cost per gigabyte are primary concerns. HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) is a 3D-stacked technology that uses through-silicon vias to connect multiple dies and offers much higher bandwidth per stack — the chapter quotes HBM2 at about 307 GB/s per stack and HBM3 numbers that are even larger. HBM delivers the bandwidth needed by GPUs and AI accelerators, but it is more expensive, offers lower capacity per stack, and increases packaging and thermal complexity. LPDDR is optimized for low power in mobile devices, balancing bandwidth and power efficiency. The practical trade-off decision depends on the workload: bandwidth-bound AI training favors HBM despite cost and capacity limits, while workloads needing large address spaces or lower cost lean toward DDR. A key misconception is thinking HBM always wins; in many servers and laptops, DDR provides a better balance of capacity and cost. Always match the technology to the workload’s bandwidth appetite and capacity needs.

keyIdea.title: Technology trade-offs
keyIdea.text: DDR offers capacity and lower cost; HBM delivers very high bandwidth at higher cost and lower per-stack capacity. LPDDR prioritizes power savings for mobile.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › DDR vs HBM vs LPDDR
DDR
Lower per-byte cost, higher capacity, moderate bandwidth, used for general-purpose systems.
HBM
3D-stacked high bandwidth via TSVs. Much higher GB/s per stack, higher cost and thermal density, used for GPUs and accelerators.
LPDDR
Low-power DDR for mobile devices, balancing bandwidth with energy efficiency and thermal constraints.
Real-world decision
Choose HBM when sustained, very high bandwidth is critical and cost/thermal constraints are acceptable. Choose DDR when capacity and cost matter more. Use LPDDR for power-limited mobile designs.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's consolidate the essential ideas. First, DRAM is dense and economical but slower than SRAM because each bit uses a capacitor and requires refresh; this creates a bandwidth and latency trade-off. Second, the DRAM organization into ranks, banks, rows and columns shapes parallelism: row buffers enable fast repeated accesses while bank conflicts and row misses reduce throughput. Third, memory bandwidth is computed from bytes per transfer, transfers per second and number of channels — use that formula to compute theoretical peaks and compare to workload requirements. Fourth, the memory controller uses open/close policies, bank interleaving and request reordering to trade off throughput and latency and to manage fairness. Finally, different memory technologies — DDR, HBM and LPDDR — make different trade-offs among bandwidth, capacity, cost and power. Keep these concepts in mind when you profile systems and when you must decide whether to invest in more channels, a faster DDR, or an HBM-equipped accelerator.

keyIdea.title: Chapter summary
keyIdea.text: Remember DRAM structure, the ACT/CAS/PRE cycle, bandwidth calculation, controller policies, and the practical trade-offs between DDR, HBM and LPDDR.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Key Concepts
DRAM vs SRAM
Transistor counts, speed, density, refresh and use cases.
Organization
Ranks, banks, rows and columns set parallelism and row buffer behavior.
Bandwidth vs Latency
Bandwidth is throughput (GB/s); latency is time for a single access (ns). Both influence performance differently.
Takeaway
Use organization and bandwidth math together to determine whether a workload is bandwidth-limited, latency-limited, or both.

narration.text: A final compact summary to anchor the most actionable ideas: First, the ACT/CAS/PRE sequence and the role of row buffers determine the latency difference between row hits and misses. Second, the memory controller can improve aggregate throughput through open-page or close-page policies, bank interleaving, and request reordering, but these choices affect fairness and latency. Third, HBM delivers orders of magnitude more GB/s per stack than DDR but at higher cost and with lower per-stack capacity; DDR remains the cost-effective choice for large memory systems. Keep these points visible when you measure performance and when you estimate whether to add channels, choose DDR5, or adopt HBM for an accelerator. Asking whether your workload processes many bytes per second or whether it needs fast single accesses helps you pick the right memory design.

keyIdea.title: Practical memory design
keyIdea.text: Match memory technology and controller policy to your workload's bandwidth and latency profile to achieve balanced system performance.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Key Concepts (Continued)
ACT / CAS / PRE
The timed sequence that drives DRAM access cost and explains row hits vs misses.
Controller policies
Open-page, close-page, interleaving and reordering shape throughput and fairness.
HBM vs DDR
HBM gives higher bandwidth per stack; DDR gives more capacity and lower cost per GB.
Final reflection
Will memory bandwidth remain the primary bottleneck for your workload, or can better layout and controller policies close the gap? Use measurements and the formulas here to decide.
